opus-5.5.text:
I think we're honestly still quite early. Everyone agrees that a world model should let an agent predict what happens next, especially as a consequence of its own actions, but there's very little consensus on what the architecture should actually be.

Right now I see roughly three camps. The first comes out of video generation: train a large diffusion or autoregressive model on huge amounts of video, add action conditioning, and hope the physics and object permanence emerge from scale. The results look impressive visually, but when you push them on consistency, like walking away from a room and coming back, or doing something causally precise, they often break. Looking realistic and being a correct simulator are different things.

The second camp says you shouldn't predict pixels at all. You should predict in a learned latent space and model only what matters for decision-making, which is the JEPA-style argument. I find that intellectually appealing, but it's harder to evaluate, and so far it hasn't produced the kind of obvious, demo-able leap that the generative approach has.

The third camp is more hybrid. It brings in explicit structure, like 3D representations, memory, or even pieces of a physics engine, and uses learning to fill in the rest. That tends to be more controllable and consistent, but people worry it won't scale the way end-to-end methods do.

What I think is genuinely unresolved is a few core questions. What should the state representation be? How do you get long-horizon memory and consistency without the cost blowing up? And maybe most importantly, how do we even measure whether a world model is good? Until we have evaluations tied to downstream use, for robotics, for agents, for planning, rather than just how the video looks, it's hard to say which architecture is winning.

So my honest view is that the field is in a pre-paradigm phase, a bit like language modeling before the Transformer became the default. I suspect the eventual answer will combine large-scale generative pretraining with some explicit memory and structure, but I'd hold that view loosely. There's still a lot of room for someone to find the right abstraction.

r001.rationale: The response says the field is still early and there is “very little consensus” on what a world model’s architecture should be.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think we're still at a very early stage. If you look at how people talk about world models right now, the term itself is doing a lot of work. Some people mean a video generation model that can predict the next frame. Some people mean a latent dynamics model in the JEPA sense, where you never reconstruct pixels at all and you only predict in an abstract representation space. Some people mean a simulator you can roll out inside of for planning, the way an agent in a game engine would. These are quite different objects, and the fact that they all share one name tells you the field hasn't converged.

So the way I'd frame it: there are a few real axes of disagreement, and I don't think any of them are settled.

The first is pixel space versus latent space. The video generation camp says, look, if you can generate coherent minutes of video with consistent physics, you have implicitly learned a world model, and scaling will take care of the rest. The latent camp says that's wasteful, that most of the bits in a video are irrelevant to decision making, and you should only predict what matters. I find the latent argument intellectually cleaner, but the empirical results right now are mostly on the generative side, because that's where the compute and data have gone. That's not the same as being right, but it's hard to ignore.

The second axis is whether a world model should be a separate module at all, or whether it just emerges inside a large enough sequence model. The language model people will tell you a transformer trained on enough text already has a rough model of the world embedded in it. The robotics people will tell you that's a model of how people describe the world, not of how the world actually behaves when you push on it, and those are very different things. I lean toward the second view. Language is a compressed, lossy record of reality. If you want a model that understands that a cup falls off a table, you probably need to have seen a lot of cups falling, not a lot of sentences about cups.

The third thing, and I think this gets underrated, is the interface to action. A world model that only predicts is a weather forecast. A world model you can act inside of, that lets you ask "what happens if I do this," is a different beast. Most of the architectures being proposed right now are much stronger on the prediction side than on the counterfactual, intervention side. And that's where planning and agency live.

If I'm being candid, I think the architecture question is a bit downstream of a data question that nobody has solved. We have a lot of internet video, but it's passive. Nobody is acting in it in a way the model can observe and control. Embodied data, where action and consequence are coupled, is scarce. So a lot of the architectural arguments are really proxies for arguments about what data you believe will become available.

My own guess is that the eventual answer looks hybrid. A latent predictive core for efficiency and planning, a generative decoder you can turn on when you need to inspect or ground what the model believes, and a tight coupling to action rather than pure observation. But I hold that loosely. Five years ago I'd have given you a confident answer about architecture and been wrong, so now I try to be confident about the questions and modest about the answers.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the field is still at a very early stage, has not converged, and that the key architectural disagreements are unsettled.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s still a very open question. Even the term “world model” can mean different things. Are we talking about a model that predicts the next observation, or one that learns an underlying state of the world and can predict how that state changes when you take an action? Those goals don’t necessarily lead to the same architecture.

One approach is to predict directly in observation space—for example, generating future video. Another is to predict in a learned latent space, where you try to capture the information that matters without reconstructing every pixel. The challenge there is deciding what matters. A representation can be good for prediction and still miss something essential for control.

So I wouldn’t say we’ve converged on an architecture. To me, the central questions are about memory, actions, uncertainty, and abstraction: what does the model need to remember, how does it represent possible futures, and can it reason over different timescales? The architecture should support those capabilities, but we also need tasks and evaluations that tell us whether it’s actually learning them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the question is still open and that researchers have not converged on a world-model architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s still a very open research question. We don’t yet have a settled definition of what a world model needs to represent, so it’s hard to say what the architecture should be. Are we trying to predict future observations, understand the underlying state of an environment, or simulate what happens when an agent takes an action? Those objectives overlap, but they don’t necessarily lead to the same design.

For me, the interesting question is where you put the structure. How much should the architecture explicitly encode things like objects, space, time, and actions, and how much can emerge from learning? You want useful inductive biases, but you also don’t want to constrain the model so much that it can’t capture the complexity of the world.

Ultimately, I’d judge these architectures by whether they support useful prediction and planning. Can the model anticipate the consequences of an action, handle unfamiliar situations, and represent uncertainty? That seems like a more meaningful test than whether its generated futures simply look convincing.

r001.rationale: The response calls the architecture question “still a very open research question” and says there is no settled definition of what a world model needs to represent.
